Joe Muranyi
Clarinetist Joe Muranyi was born in Martin’s Ferry, Ohio on January 14, 1928.
He has worked as a record producer for major labels and played alongside Roy Eldridge, Jimmy McPartland and Max Kaminsky. Joe was a member of the Louis Armstrong All-Stars from 1967-1971.
Joe was interviewed in New York City on January 11, 2007 by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive. Tim Hicks and Vince Giordano participated briefly in the interview.
My name is Monk Rowe and we’re in Manhattan at the International Association of Jazz Educators conference. I’m pleased to have Joe Muranyi with me this afternoon. Did I pronounce your name good?
Yeah that’s pretty good.
In Hungary they do it different, is that right?
In Hungary, I wouldn’t say it’s a common name but everybody pronounces it correctly: mu-ray-nee is how they say it.
Well in reading about you it seems like an interesting trip from balalaika orchestras to Lenny Tristano to Louis Armstrong to what you’re doing now.

Well that balalaika is one of those things, you know, you say something that’s off-beat or not in the normal events in the course of normal events, and that triggers up. Yeah. When I was going to college, you know, I went to Columbia and Manhattan School of Music, I sort of gigged around. I played with, I actually played with an old time Italian band, you know a street band sort of. We didn’t play in the street, but it was in Springfield, Mass. in some Catholic church basement. And that was an experience you know. You had no music, these old guys, it’s like the equivalent New Orleans or something. And they played standard classical repertoire and they had flute, clarinet, oboe, you know, it was like, the balalaikas were like the violins and the violas and all that stuff. And they played classical stuff and Glinka and things like that from the Russian days. And they also played Russian folk songs (sings) which was ethnic again. It was kind of fun.
Well it’s a great mix for your ears to be doing all that kind of stuff, right?

Oh yeah. I love so-called ethnic music you know. I used to have quite a collection of klezmer stuff, which I like very much, and there again, the earlier the better. In the twenty-something it was just wonderful. The new klezmer bands well they’re fun and stuff but they don’t have the level of anything like the old timers did.
Was music a big part of your household when you were young? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Yeah I think so. My parents were musical. They sang and — they didn’t play any instruments, nor in my mother’s family there were a lot of brothers and sisters, they didn’t play anything. But I recently learned that my grandfather, my father’s father, played violin and guitar which was a surprise to me. I barely remember him. But they were always musical, and I always thought that, you know, Hungarians had a natural affinity for music like Italians, Irish, something like that. And in recent years, the past 20 years or so, I’ve gone there a lot and I find that I was basing my opinion of Hungarians on my parents and my family. Because not all black people have rhythm, no. It’s very similar. You know. So but music was a very important part and you know I’m getting to the age where I’ve had thoughts and funny thoughts and I cheer up easily. And I’m an emotional being. Of course we all are. But the other night, there was something about “Pennies From Heaven.” The song came up. And I had this recall of, I have two grandkids, George and Charles. And George is seven and Charles is five. And they’re musical, I could tell right away. They can carry a tune when they hear something. And I’m thinking about myself, you know, at what age did I start thinking about the music and considering music and whatever. And I remembered that I learned “Pennies From Heaven” [sings] every time it rains it rains — to this day I mean I know the words very well — directly connected back to when I was six or seven. And so I used to go to the movies on Saturday morning for a nickel in those days, you know, in Martin’s Ferry, Ohio, Bellaire, Ohio, way far away like that. Steel mines and coal mines and a lot of the immigrant bohunks you know and all that kind of stuff. Polacks and Italians. So I used to go to the movies. I might have seen it there, and maybe I heard it on the radio. My parents at that time didn’t have a gramophone, so I learned “Pennies From Heaven” because I liked it and my ear. And the words and all. And they used to stand me up, that’s the only one I remember, stand me up onto the chair, like seven years old, and I would perform.
You’d do that song.

You know so I said gee, I guess I must have a calling — I’m not saying a great calling — but it must mean something to me. And so as a kid I was very aware of music. I heard the Hungarian music, you know, my parents used to go to dances and balls and picnics and they’d have a gypsy band. And that I liked. I mean I just listened. It didn’t occur to me that it was different or funny or anything, I’d listen and I was just open to it. And I found that I enjoyed most the bass player. And they had like a German bow, you know, you put your fingers right in it? The frog you know, it looked about like that. It comes down and they put their fingers in at the end of it.
Um, they really grab it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
Yeah. Zoom — zoom — zoom. And I’d just stand in front of them and I enjoyed that so much. And I’ll tell you there’s a funny thing. You ever hear of a trombone player named Cutty Cutshall?
Sure.

I knew Cutty. I played with him you know, more than a few times at the Eddie Condon’s in midtown in the 50s. And somehow we got onto this. And it turns out he was from eastern Pennsylvania or something like that, you know I was born in Martin’s Ferry, which is on the Ohio River down the river from Pittsburgh a hundred miles or not even that. And he was from that area, and he too, even though he didn’t have the Hungarian background, he too loved the gypsy bands and the bass player going zoom — zoom — zoom. So it was a funny kind of thing.
You would have been pretty young during the Depression.
Oh yeah.
Do you have any recollection of that being a particularly hard time for your family or your neighborhood?

Yeah well you know my parents were immigrants and we were poor but I didn’t know it. My mother was such a handy housekeeper and she cooked and cleaned and baked, and you know it was just sort of — and my father was a steel worker, he worked in the steel mill and stuff, and that was, I remember that was the era of the unions organizing you know, which was very critical. I mean today I know maybe unions are considered Mafia run and all that, but in my estimation there’s a great room in America for labor unions and what labor unions do. And so I remember when I had a friend who was very teary and crying and he said one day his father had been beaten to death by company goons with a baseball bat, because they wanted to strike or something like that. So I remember that and I remember my father was out on the left wing you know. I remember that he was very involved in politics in the sense of voting for somebody or campaigning for somebody you know. And there was a famous — well to me a famous — governor Davey I think it was, I don’t know I think in the 30s. And there was a lot of campaigning against him. And he had some sort of tar road plan and so on. And somehow he had something to swindle about tarring, making asphalt roads or whatever you know. So yes, I have a very strong and vivid memory of the Depression and to this day I love old movies made as contemporary movies in the 30s, and the earlier the better. They’re very interesting because they reflect the time. And I get that feeling from them.
Were your parents wanting you to get a trade, a craft that would make a nice life for you?

Well that develops — I was going to take accordion lessons from my father — not my father, a friend of my father’s, some Italian guy. And I never got to handle an accordion ever, and I took lessons for three or four months. It was all solfeggio on a grand scale and © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
all of that, you know, it was like I’m dying to get my hands on something. So I don’t know what happened.
Oh you mean you were taking lessons and you never even got to play one for a while.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I don’t remember if I had solfeggio or singing, maybe, but it was grand staff, the do-re-me-fa-so-la-C and all that kind of stuff, and I guess I sort of forgot it because — I don’t know, maybe it had some early — and then I was going to take violin lessons. There was a guy named Pragia who came from Cleveland. And I don’t think he was a gypsy, he was just sort of a very artistic, very, a fairly young guy with pale skin and very delicate fingers and was a hell of a violin player. And I had like one lesson or something or two lessons, and he was letting me hold it and things like that, and he stopped coming to Martin’s Ferry. I think he had like a route he’d do, he’d come and teach the Hungarian community, and he’d teach kids. So he disappeared so that was that. So they wanted a musical education for me, they didn’t want me to be a musician particularly. They were good parents. My father wasn’t a drunk or you know, like he was a respectable family man, he had to provide for his family. And later on when I was a teenager he wanted me to be an electrician. He had a friend that was an electrician in the union and he could have gotten me into the union at age 17 or 18 or whatever like that, which is like guaranteeing you a lifetime income you know. And I wasn’t interested, no I was interested in music, and that didn’t appeal to me you know. Idiot. I always wondered what would have happened had I done it. I think I still would have been musical you know. As a young musician’s life, as we all know, is not the most secure in general.
That’s true. So what was the first sort of jazz-related music that caught your ear?

Well this is very interesting. If you’re sensitive to music, as I was and am and hope to be for many more years, in that environment in Ohio there, in the 30s, there was no T.V. of course, there was radio and records. I was exposed to this Hungarian music, you know, which swings you know. Gunter Schuller says you know, that jazz music swings. Jazz is the only one — no, no. Hungarian music, you know, even Romanians even, I mean talk about swing. Anyhow —
Does it have the, doing the off-beats two and four?
No, no, no.
But it has a groove to it.

It’s just, you hear it. There’s nothing but rhythm going on. I still have some Romanian LPs you know. It’s outasight. It’s a sense of rhythm and you know like odd tempos in seven and five and you know. Well so anyhow, I was exposed to this Hungarian music. And then I was exposed to the swing era, you know swing music, the big bands you know, that business [scats] sophisticated swing you know. I have a vivid memory of walking through a carnival kind of thing, an outdoor thing, with my mother, late at night. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Maybe we were walking to go home or something, I don’t know how. And over the P.A. system came that. And I liked that, and I said yeah. Years later when I heard it I said ooh I know that. So I was exposed to swing, I was exposed to Hungarian music, and then in that area there was a station, WWVA, and it had the equivalent of Grand Ole Opry. And on Saturday a midnight jamboree or something you know. And they had country players and fiddles and banjos and stuff. And so I had that influence. And so that was country- western. And then of course the Bing Crosby, the pop. Not swing but the pop tunes.
Yeah, the “Pennies From Heaven” type of songs.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. So it was all around me, and I wasn’t necessarily in the cradle of the blues or anything like that. But that’s a funny one. I mean you’ll hear young black guys, I have my own ideas about the origin of jazz, I don’t think it’s black. It’s not a black music, it’s an American music. There was always white and Irishmen and Italians and stuff. And if you’re black and you want to be proud about your black rhythm, that’s marvelous, that’s great, some of the greatest were you know. Joe Oliver, Louis Armstrong, Johnny Dodds. So but anyhow what was I saying? Oh so the midnight jamboree, and all that kind of music, and as a matter of fact my kid singing I continued with that, and they had an amateur contest on WWVA. And really, and I went to it, they had an audition at the amateur contest. And I go down with my mother and, you know we have no music or anything like that, and it was like something from “Our Gang.”
Like “Our Gang,” yeah.
And there was a row of kids with their mothers.
All dressed up probably?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. There was a skinny little red-haired girl, she might have had freckles even, she was singing and she had a violin you know. And it came her turn, and in the 30s it was [scats]. Benny Goodman made a record of it, it was a pop tune [scats].
Okay.
You never heard of it, huh?
Not that one, no.

But it’s on a discography, Benny made a record and others. Bad thing. And so this little girl [screeches scats] well you could fall on the floor, even when I was a kid I said, “boy that’s pretty terrible,” scratching I mean. So we all did the thing, and I made the auditions. And I sang on the radio twice, can you imagine? Now I don’t remember whether it was the Amateur Hour program or whether they put the winning amateurs on some bigger program. But the strange thing was — what did I sing and how did I pick it? I haven’t the vaguest. [sings] “There’s a goldmine in the sky far away/we will find it you and I some sweet day.” Nick Kenny, you ever hear of Nick Kenny?
No. © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Nick Kenny, he was a columnist in the news or something and he wrote lyrics for songs. And this was one of his, it’s a sentimental thing, goldmine — and the other one was “There’s a goldmine in the sky far away.” So I sang them.
Did you have an accompanist?

Somebody played. Oh yeah, they had a piano player I guess. There was accompaniment. I wasn’t alone. But when I think of it I was just seven or eight. And that was sort of bizarre. And I very rarely run through this in my mind, and connecting it to later things, you know. So it started then. And then I kept singing and then my parents left Ohio — not professionally or anything, just amateur. My father had — I had only one uncle, my uncle John. And my father was sort of on the square side and John was the direct opposite, a hellion. Women loved him. Very handsome. He looked like Clark Gable sort of. And he was with a Hungarian dance company. And he sang and danced professionally. And the first time he heard me sing “Pennies From Heaven” he comes up to me and he says you know that thing you sang in there? That’s not in the song. I said well I just sort of like that.
You were already improvising.

I did a little something, but he caught me on it. And to myself I said well I don’t care what he thinks, it sounds okay to me. But so he was musical so there must have been some musical feeling on my father’s side, on my father’s side of the family. Time went by, we moved to New York, and my mother I guess was a show biz mother in her own way, you never figure to think about it, but we came to New York and she somehow found a studio or something that gave kids vocal lessons and it was on Broadway — getting to the big time — Broadway, 52nd, 51st, 53rd Street. You go upstairs you know, and I went up there was a woman, and I don’t know whether she played the piano or whether it was a guy that played the piano, and we sang songs. And I remember I had the sheet music for [sings] You are the promised kiss of springtime — you know that thing.
“All the Things You Are.”
So I sang through that. So I mean isn’t that funny, I had to re-learn that many a time.
Do we need to stop, Tim? TH: Yes, please. I need to move this. When you shift you’re getting pinched here and I’m going to bring this around the others side.
Yeah that’s a tricky tune.
Yeah I mean it’s got very nice changes, but you’ve really got to know them. I’ve been on the rocks more than once with it.
Yeah, right.
At Jimmy Ryan’s. I mean Bobby Pratt, the wonderful trombone player and piano player, he played the hell out of it with Roy Eldridge you know like that, he knew the sucker. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
Right. So you did “All the Things You Are.” It does have that, getting about halfway through it’s got that —
Oh yeah, yeah [scats] it goes somewhere else.
It goes somewhere else.
Are we on the air? TH: Yup.

So I did that, and I don’t remember particularly performing as performing, but I was taking these lessons, you know, maybe a couple of years of once a week or once every two weeks you know. And I did it and I don’t know what it cost but they had to pay money you know. And my father was not making a lot of money, it was Depression times you know. And then my father belonged to a lodge in the Bronx. We lived in the Bronx. And they had a band, a small band. And they were looking for recruits. So — what was her name, there was a little Eva or Emma, something or other. And they were Hungarians you know. And she cornered me and said what did I want to play — would I like to join the band. I said well —. She said, “what would you like to play, the tuba?” You know.
Yeah they needed a tuba, right?

Yeah, like that. I said no. I never thought of it. No, no, no. She said well trumpet? And she said clarinet? And you know I must have been pretty hip already or something, but I immediately thought of Artie Shaw or Benny Goodman. “Yeah, the clarinet.” It’s very funny you know. And Woody Herman. I knew Woody Herman a little and I told him this story. And I said you’re one of the guys responsible. Matter of fact I told Benny Goodman too. You’re one of the guys responsible for me.
Really?

And I met Artie Shaw, I knew Artie Shaw a little you know. I never told him but I believe with that sort of thing you’ve got to tell people. So it was clarinet. And her name was List, I forget his first name, Mr. List I called him. Very nice man. He was sort of like the violin teacher , slight, pale, very musical. I don’t know what he played. But he was a very good teacher in that he taught me fingerings. I mean to this day, you know, the high notes and everything. You know like really correct. The alternates, and how to get around. As a matter of fact I remember, this is very funny, that I played the Carters’ inaugural with the World’s Greatest Jazz Band. And it was a Duke Ellington band, it wasn’t the real band, it was like the band after the band after the band. As a matter of fact while we were performing for Jimmy Carter I guess it was, they had a fist fight in the band.
Oh good.
In Duke’s band and God knows what. And the clarinet player comes to me after the thing and he says, “how do you finger a high G?” And I showed him I mean. But certainly Mr. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

List was a very good teacher. But I went home and I had a clarinet, it costs 25 bucks. And we paid it off a dollar a week or two dollars a week or something like that. And I wasn’t an instant success with it because I went home and I was going to master this sucker you know. And I had a younger sister —I had, she’s passed on — and she was musical, she danced. She did Hungarian folk dancing, really good. And as a matter of fact her teacher was this old lady, it was Mrs. Serly, and her son was Tibor Serly, who finished the Bartok whatever it is, you know, there was a guy, Tibor Serly finished I think the Bartok Concerto or something. When Bartok died before it was finished he finished it. And he used to play piano for their dancing. Remember him, I said, you know who that was? Well anyway, where was I?
How did you make your first dollar with your clarinet?

Oh, oh, oh. Well this is very deep. So anyhow, well let me finish the story about my sister. So I went home with the clarinet and I started to practice and she laughed and said “you sound like a duck,” which led me to practice. And I evidently improved very quickly. I mean I just ate it up. So then I ended up in high school and I played in the high school band. And I never got into athletics much, you know, football. “You’d make a good football player” you know. I wanted to play the clarinet. So my first dollar with the clarinet, would you believe, was a gig in Trenton, New Jersey and the bass player was Pops Foster. It was a bowling alley in Trenton, New Jersey. I think it paid a lot of money, like 35 bucks or something, which was a lot of money.
Apiece?
Yeah.
That’s a lot of money at that time.

Yeah, well when was it, late 40s, 50s? Well late 40s I guess. And it was a very funny one because we were in this place and we go down, there’s a restaurant in the place, in the bowling alley, and we’re going to have something to eat. And it was Pops Foster. And I knew who he was, I loved him and I respected him you know. And he looks at the menu and he said, “is this every tub?” I said, “Pops, what’s every tub?” “Oh,” he says, “don’t you know what that means?” I said, “no.” He said, “every tub on its own bottom, do we pay or does the boss pay?” And then you know there’s a King Oliver record called “Every Tub.”
Sure there is. And a Basie record too.

Yeah, yeah. And there’s — I think I heard Louis Armstrong say a couple of times, you know an ensemble when you start playing? “Every tub.” You know, it’d be every guy on his own, you know, going to improvise.
So he meant everybody was paying for their own food?
Everybody on his own. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
Everybody on his own.
By every tub means every tub on its own bottom. Everybody on his own.
That’s cool.
Okay? And that could apply to paying or it could apply to improvising. You know we’re not going to read music or don’t play the melody, unison. Improvise, yeah.
Right. That’s great. I love learning that lingo.

Oh there’s many things. And I have sort of a historical and scientific — not deeply historical because I love history, it was my favorite subject in school. But I remember the little details. I’m an encyclopedia about pulling teeth. I connect one thing to another and I love that every tub thing. Because it carried all the way through to Louis Armstrong you know. So anyhow, that was in Trenton. I’m trying to think — there’s a guy named Irving Kratka, played the drums. He started a record label, what was it?
Oh Inner City Records.
Yeah, and “Music Minus One.”
Irv Kratka? I’ll be darned.
Yeah.
“Music Minus One.”
That was my idea.
Oh get out.

It was, yeah. I started a record company with him and then, well it’s too long a story. But I made a list of possible ideas for a small record company that the big ones aren’t doing so much, and that was one of them. I mean who would have known? I mean he actually followed it through, but it was something a small company could do that bigger ones don’t. So anyhow the music continues and you know I still consider myself a musician, I mean that’s what I’ve been doing for the sole of my existence for a long time now. And I am odd in that my generation usually by this time has been playing bebop for a long time. You know, and they sort of came up in the late big band era, playing saxophone or something in a big band and then went on, you know, and the lingua franca of the day was bebop. You know? Swing wasn’t that strong. But I didn’t come up that way. You know I’m too young to have been part of the scene in the 30s to play in the big bands, and I am an old revivalist. You know after World War II there were the moldy figs, the ones that were interested in old records and King Oliver and Jelly Roll Morton and that kind of stuff, you know going back to the original. That was me. I loved that. And so in high school I belonged to the Brooklyn Tech Jazz Society and we’d bring in records and I junk shopped you know, and nothing was available, Monk. Today it’s like the computer — you can get everything, even that Red Hot Jazz Archive you can go on, you know that? © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
Um hum.
You know there it is, I would have killed for those records and you just click on them. How were you going to get them?
Did it make it more precious for you?
Yes.
Because it was something you had to really aspire to get and figure out how to get and carry the 78s home and all that stuff.

Oh yeah. Junk shopping I remember I was in Washington, D.C. I went to the Army Air Corps, which became the Air Force just as I left, band school. In Bolling Field. And my uncle, Uncle John, the musical one, lived there and his wife was a nurse there at St. Elizabeth or something. And Anacostia was there, the big black neighborhood. And I remember one day I went out and it was unbelievable, there were like rarity, like treasures. God I went out and I found a Johnny Dodds Paramount record in very good shape. You could see Dixieland Thumpers and I found a Freddie Keppard record. I mean, and it was a gold mine. And New York had been picked out. There were a lot of big collectors here you know, they had been picked out and were very hard to find anymore. But I did, I even went door to door, you know in the black neighborhoods in the afternoon, “I’m looking for old records, have you any old records?” Sometimes I found them.
You’re kidding.
So it was very precious.
Wow. And you got to play during your military service, you got to continue to play?

Oh yeah, yeah. So I played in the band and then it was like, I think it was like 1946 or something, and I graduated high school and it was a matter of — when I joined the Air Force the war was still on. The war didn’t technically end until ’47 or something, by treaty or whatever. So I enlisted in ’46 and I’m a veteran of World War II ‘cause the war was still on. But I was going to get drafted. They were still drafting then, they hadn’t changed that law. So I don’t know why — I mean I was always, I’m not a bad businessman but I’m not ahead, I’m not. And somehow I got the information that if you enlisted for three years, and then you would get the GI bill and you could go to college. And if you enlisted then you could pick what you wanted to be. So I enlisted and I wanted to be a bandsman. I was promised that so I enlisted. And I’d go to San Antonio, Texas for, and even then I junk shopped and I found some records. I went over — there’s a river in San Antonio and a couple of waterfalls. I almost went over one of the waterfalls in my khaki outfit with a rowboat or something.
Oh really. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

But anyhow, and talking about career choices — will I be an electrician or not — so there I am and I took all the exams and stuff. And one day Private Marino or whatever they called me — “yeah.” “You’ve got to go down to headquarters.” And I thought what did I do? As a matter of fact I did do something when they trained us. You know, hip — hip — hip to the left, right, right oblique, all that kind of stuff. And okay, cigarette break, 15 minutes or something. And we’d all sit down. And I pulled out a book, I’m reading a book, and the sergeant comes over. “What the F are you doing?” I said, “I’m reading a book.” He said, “you’re not allowed to read a book, you’ve got to smoke a cigarette.” I said, “I don’t smoke.” And you know the next day there was a general order on the bulletin board that there will be no reading of books during —. So anyhow, and there were all like rebels, you know, like it was the end of the world. Southerners and you know, from the back woods and all that kind of stuff. So, “Muranyi — Private Muranyi.” I go down, so and so and so, sit down and the officer said, “yes.” There’s a guy, an officer, got a folder with my name. He says, “you know you have a very high IQ.” And I’m flattered, you know, I said, “well yeah, okay.” I’d had tests before and they rated pretty good. And I had gone to Brooklyn Tech which is still to this day considered a very good high school. And I did pretty good. I mean I flunked one of the math courses. It was almost calculus was what it was and non mi piace — I didn’t like it. Anyhow so he says, “you know, we’re always looking for bright young men” he says, “how would you like to go to cryptography school?” So I says, “oh no, no, no, no.” I want to be a clarinet player. I was promised that MOS — military occupation specialty — 508 or whatever it was. And he said, “you know it wouldn’t be bad, we’d send you to Washington and etcetera, etcetera you know. And I said no, no. And I always thought suppose I had said yes.
That’s like figuring out codes and all that.

Yeah, yeah. I’d be probably a CIA guy or something. Isn’t that funny? I mean I know it was a choice you know. So I was put into the band and I was stationed in Westover Field in Springfield, Mass in a Military Air Transport Command — MATS. And I played in the band and they ran the — you know from Westover they used to go to Germany, I can’t think of the name of it, it’s still there, the Air Force base. Wiesbaden, and then there was the name of a Air Force base. And they’d go back and forth and stuff. And they even had a choice of that, did I want to go. I should have done that too. In Germany after the war would be very nice you know, I’d probably speak some German you know, probably would have grabbed some German chick for all I know. But anyhow, I played in a band and had a wonderful time. And I was there for three years, I made Sergeant, and they promised me Staff Sergeant if I re-upped and I went no, I hated the Army. But I was the band librarian and I had some decision on what we were going to play, with the First Sergeant who conducted, Sergeant Baraka was a doll. Right. I’ll think of that in a moment.

Yeah, yeah, “I Got Rhythm” you know. A twelve inch V-disk. He played that for me and a couple of other things you know. It was very nice. So I had a very good time. A lot of red notes.

So he called me in and he says, “you like the trumpet?” And Paul says, “yeah.” Well a conversation ensued and then he said, “I sat on the bed next to him and he says ‘you want to blow it?’” And I mean the old man fell in love with my son you know. He never had any kids you know what I mean? So I mean I remember a couple of nights in Reno and Pops was kind of bombed. We were at the blackjack table. And he starts on a monologue on me and my son: “boy he’s got Joe Muranyi on clarinet man, he’s got a son, you ought to see that little sucker.” Whatever. It was darling. So anyhow he impressed Paul. And Paul and two of my daughters, they’re both very artistic, my daughter’s better but my son’s pretty good. And for years Paul drew a head with teeth, a big smile. It was obviously Pops. And at the time I didn’t pick up on it. It’s this big smile and he called it “Louie Lightbulb.” I mean it’s like when Pops is around a light goes on. But it was so darling you know. That’s the “Louie Lightbulb” story.
Gee that’s a neat story. Well you said in a little note you wrote to me, you said as far as your own career right now, you said thank God for Europe.
Yeah.
You go over there a lot?

Yeah. I mean they have jazz, not everywhere, but generally jazz is considered more of a cultural thing, more art. And you know George Bernard Shaw or somebody said that if you travel and go to foreign countries that’s the only time you get to know your own country you know. And America, I am an American, I love America, I was born here and went to school here you know. I served in the armed forces here as I said before. But there’s an awful lot — America’s not perfect you know. There are a lot of traits America has that — we’re just so big you know that we don’t take criticism easily. And there are many aspects. So in Europe, I think jazz is getting less there too than it is here, frankly I think rock has taken over. But I find that I’m more appreciated and I get more work and more surprising — I walk down a small street in Hungary or something and everybody knows in the street who I am. And it’s not, I don’t know what that is but it makes you feel © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-
good. And I’m not expecting people to stop in the street, who am I after all, a clarinet player. But I get a much better feeling out of Europe, being a musician there.
You expressed some feelings about jazz education before we started today.
Jazz what?
Jazz education?

Oh yeah. Well I don’t think there’s anything wrong with somebody going to a conservatory to study music and to study jazz. But I’ve never yet met a program, I mean just consider what they produce. They produce people that know about Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker and pros and everything like that. And I guess some courses they treat history. But forget it. And then they all play the latest thing — oh about the definition of jazz. It’s got to have freedom, yeah. And I like the idea of modern jazz and what they produce but I don’t actually like the music you know. It’s a very curious thing. As I said before, if somebody just asked me do I like jazz, I say no, because I know what they’re thinking and I don’t like it. And let’s put it this way: jazz is so compartmentalized. There are so many aspects. And America’s got this bad history of antagonism between the styles of jazz. You know in Norway I went to a party celebrating somebody’s thirtieth anniversary in the business and all the jazz musicians were there: the modern, the beboppers, they were all there and they gave somebody an award and they all had a drink and had a meal. You know, and that felt very un-American. I’m sorry to say it, especially in New York they just dice and slice each other you know. But maybe because work is so scarce.
Yeah. Did you ever have any issues with traveling in an integrated group when you were with Louis?
No.
We’ll take a short pause here. I think this is a fellow you might know actually.
Who’s that.
Hi come on in.
Oh Joe Muranyi, don’t believe anything he says.
I’m trying not to.
Hey did you get my email?
Is this on the film?
This is on the film now.
Oh Jesus I’m sorry.
That’s all right. We’re just wrapping up. You guys can just — we’re a little cramped here. TH: We were supposed to have a suite and this is what we have.
Great to see you, Vinnie, I think you deserve to be interviewed man. © Fillius Jazz Archive -24-
Well I don’t know about that.
Yeah, go on.
I’m trying to remember what we were talking about.
About jazz, about liking jazz or not liking jazz. Well there was some factor you were going to.
The jazz education we were talking about — oh I know, I was just wondering about when you traveled with Louis, that the group was integrated, if it ever became an issue traveling anywhere.
You mean the fact that he was black or that it was a mixed band?
Yes, it was a mixed band.

No. By the time I was there, I heard him refer, he’d meet some of his old buddies would come up and there was one he was talking about, I had $2,000 in my pocket, he said, and I had no place to sleep or eat or anything. So that came up, but art, you know, art actually.
Well it’s been really fascinating.
Okay.
I enjoyed talking to you and I wish you the best of luck.
I need a miracle.
You’re going back overseas soon? You have something scheduled?
Oh I think in June I’ve got something. There’s an annual Louis Armstrong festival, this is the third annual.
I see.
And I’m sort of the jovial emcee in Hungarian.
Okay. Well thank you.
Okay Rowe, Monk Rowe, it’s nice talking with you.
My pleasure.
I hope you got enough.
I did. © Fillius Jazz Archive -25-

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Opening and the pronunciation of Muranyi
segments.summary: Monk Rowe introduces the interview at the IAJE conference and asks how Muranyi is pronounced in Hungary.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Playing in an Italian balalaika band; love of ethnic music
segments.summary: Muranyi recalls gigging in a street-style band in a Springfield church basement and his fondness for old klezmer and ethnic music.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Musical parents and singing 'Pennies From Heaven' as a child
segments.summary: His parents and grandfather were musical; at six or seven he learned 'Pennies From Heaven' and performed it standing on a chair.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Gypsy band bass players and Cutty Cutshall
segments.summary: He loved the bass player in the Hungarian gypsy bands and finds that trombonist Cutty Cutshall shared the same fondness.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Growing up in the Depression, steelworker father and unions
segments.summary: Poor immigrant family in Martin's Ferry; his father was a union-minded steelworker and he recalls labor violence and politics.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Accordion and violin lessons, father's wish for an electrician
segments.summary: Early lessons on accordion and violin fizzled out, and his father wanted him to become a union electrician.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: First musical influences: Hungarian music, swing, country and pop
segments.summary: He describes the Hungarian, swing, WWVA country and pop music around him, and his view that jazz is American rather than black music.

segments.chapter: Childhood in Ohio and first music
segments.title: Singing on the WWVA amateur hour and Uncle John
segments.summary: As a child he auditioned and sang on WWVA radio, and his dancer uncle John noticed him improvising on a song.

segments.chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
segments.title: Vocal lessons in New York and 'All the Things You Are'
segments.summary: After the move to New York his mother put him in a Broadway vocal studio; talk turns to the difficulty of 'All the Things You Are'.

segments.chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
segments.title: Lodge band, choosing the clarinet and teacher Mr. List
segments.summary: A Bronx lodge band recruiter offered him instruments and he chose clarinet inspired by Shaw and Goodman; Mr. List taught him fingerings.

segments.chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
segments.title: Practicing with his sister, high school band, first paid gig
segments.summary: His sister's teasing spurred practice; he played in high school band and mentions his first paid gig in Trenton.

segments.chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
segments.title: Pops Foster and the meaning of 'every tub'
segments.summary: On the Trenton bowling alley gig Pops Foster explains 'every tub on its own bottom', meaning paying or improvising for yourself.

segments.chapter: New York, the clarinet and first gigs
segments.title: Irving Kratka, Music Minus One and becoming a revivalist
segments.summary: He claims the Music Minus One idea for Kratka and says he is an old revivalist who loved early jazz records in the Brooklyn Tech Jazz Society.

segments.chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
segments.title: Junk-shopping for 78s, including Washington, D.C.
segments.summary: Hunting rare records was hard work; he found Dodds and Keppard records while stationed in Washington, going door to door.

segments.chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
segments.title: Enlisting in the Air Force and refusing cryptography school
segments.summary: He enlisted to be a bandsman and turned down an offer to train in cryptography after high test scores.

segments.chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
segments.title: Military band at Westover Field, V-disks and first jazz playing
segments.summary: He played clarinet in the Air Transport Command band, heard Lester Young V-disks with Sergeant Baraka, and began to improvise.

segments.title: Nola's Studio jam sessions and meeting Bob Wilber
segments.summary: He joined New York jam sessions at Nola's Studio where he first met Bob Wilber and imitated Johnny Dodds.

segments.title: College, the Red Onions, first gigs, Tip Toe Inn and the union
segments.summary: Clarinet heroes, a fraternity improvising test, a Bridgeport gig and getting his union card amid anecdotes of union corruption.

segments.title: Getting the RCA International job and creating the RCA label
segments.summary: Through Dick Hadlock he joined RCA and helped build the catalogue of the new RCA label after the Victor trademark split.

segments.title: Stories from RCA colleagues about Bessie Smith, Louis Armstrong and Jimmie Rodgers
segments.summary: Co-workers tell him recording anecdotes about Bessie Smith, a Louis Armstrong session ruined by soot, and Jimmie Rodgers.

segments.title: Steve Sholes signs Elvis; rock and roll
segments.summary: At RCA he watched Steve Sholes sign Elvis Presley for $50,000 and discusses rock and roll's effect.

segments.title: Decline of live jazz in New York bars and clubs
segments.summary: He explains how rents, TV and changing habits killed neighborhood jazz bars and clubs.

segments.title: Meeting George Wettling and playing with McPartland and Red Allen
segments.summary: Through Wettling he joined the Condon and McPartland circle, toured with Jimmy McPartland and played with Red Allen.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson at the Stuyvesant Casino and George Lewis
segments.summary: He saw Bunk Johnson's opening night, got to know George Lewis, and assesses the band's playing and Lewis's later meeting.

segments.title: Lennie Tristano lessons and meeting Kenny Davern
segments.summary: He studied with Tristano but found modern jazz not for him, and a story is told about how he first met Kenny Davern.

segments.title: Originality in jazz and copying like Sol Yaged
segments.summary: He admires Davern's creativity and says copying choruses is a fool's errand; one must be his own person.

segments.title: Defining jazz: jazz is what Louis Armstrong plays
segments.summary: He struggles to define jazz and concludes it is the music Armstrong plays, before an audio clip of a session is played.

segments.title: Armstrong never lost his fire; Roy Eldridge, Zutty Singleton and Louis as friend
segments.summary: Armstrong kept his fire; he played with Roy Eldridge and Armstrong simultaneously, reunited Zutty and Louis, and describes Louis's warmth.

segments.title: The 'Louie Lightbulb' story with his son Paul
segments.summary: His young son charmed Armstrong in Reno, leading to his drawings of 'Louie Lightbulb'.

segments.title: Why Europe is better for him as a musician
segments.summary: He says jazz is valued more as culture in Europe, and he is recognized on the street in Hungary.

segments.title: Jazz education and the antagonism between styles
segments.summary: He criticizes jazz education and America's quarreling over jazz styles compared with Norway.

segments.title: Traveling with an integrated band and a visit from Vince Giordano
segments.summary: Asked about integrated travel with Armstrong, he says it was never an issue, after a brief interruption by a visitor.

segments.title: Closing and upcoming Armstrong festival in Hungary
segments.summary: Wrap-up, thanks, and mention of an upcoming Louis Armstrong festival where he will emcee in Hungarian.
